plan.title: Why a too-large learning rate makes gradient descent blow up
plan.description: A ball sits on a bowl-shaped loss surface. The bowl is steep in one direction and gentle in the other. On each step the ball jumps against the slope by an amount equal to the learning rate times the slope, and it leaves a trail. An arrow shows the slope (the gradient), which points uphill, and the ball always moves the other way. With a small learning rate the ball slides down into the bottom. As you raise it, the ball starts overshooting the valley floor and zigzagging. Past a threshold, each zigzag lands higher than the one before, and the ball flies off the bowl.
plan.reason: Divergence makes the most sense when you can push the learning rate past the threshold yourself and watch each step overshoot more than the last. The readouts show the number that causes it.
interactions: Change the learning rate. Below 1 ÷ steepness the ball slides straight in; between that and 2 ÷ steepness it zigzags but settles; above 2 ÷ steepness the zigzags grow and it leaves the bowl.
Change the steepness of the bowl. A steeper bowl lowers the learning rate at which descent blows up. The surface, the trail and the threshold readout all update.
Play, pause or single-step the descent and watch the trail, the slope arrow and the loss readout after each step.
Restart the descent from the same starting point, keeping your current settings and clearing the trail.
assumptions: This is an illustration: a simple made-up bowl, not a real model being trained.
The loss is 0.5 × (x² + steepness × y²). So the slope is x in the gentle direction and steepness × y in the steep direction.

Each step multiplies the distance from the bottom by (1 − learning rate) in the gentle direction and by (1 − learning rate × steepness) in the steep one. In this model, a negative multiplier means overshoot; a size above 1 means divergence. With steepness 4, that is learning rates above 0.5.
The ball starts at the same fixed point every time, off-center in both directions.
A run stops after 40 steps, or as soon as the ball leaves the drawn part of the surface. When it leaves, the card marks the run as diverged.
limitations: Real loss surfaces are not perfect bowls. In a real model the safe learning rate depends on the local curvature, which can change during training, so the threshold here is exact only for this bowl.
A diverging ball leaves the drawn area within a few steps. After that the card reports that the run diverged instead of following the ball off-screen.
There is no noise or momentum: every step uses the exact slope.
plan.learningGoal: Gradient descent diverges when the learning rate is so large that each step overshoots the valley floor by more than the starting distance. That happens once the learning rate passes 2 divided by the curvature of the steepest direction.

draft.title: Why a too-large learning rate makes gradient descent blow up
draft.description: A ball sits on a bowl-shaped loss surface. The bowl is steep left to right and gentle front to back. Each step the ball jumps against the slope by the learning rate times the slope, leaving an orange trail. A dark arrow on the ball shows the slope, which points uphill; the ball moves the opposite way. A small learning rate slides the ball in. A larger one makes it zigzag across the valley. Above 2 divided by the steepness, each zigzag lands farther out and the ball leaves the bowl.

actions.label: New run, keep old path faint

assumptions: Illustration: a made-up bowl, loss = 0.5 × (gentle² + steepness × steep²), not a real model being trained.

The slope is gentle in the front-back direction and steepness × steep in the left-right direction. Each step multiplies the distance by (1 − rate) front-back and by (1 − rate × steepness) left-right; below −1 the zigzag grows. With steepness 4 that means rates above 0.5.

The surface shows the bowl drawn at half the loss, and only out to a fixed edge: ±2 front-back and ±2/√steepness left-right. A steeper bowl is drawn narrower. Leaving that area marks the run diverged and stops it; the ball and trail are then drawn at the rim.

Converged means a loss below 0.00001. A run stops after 40 steps. Every run starts at the same point: 1.7 gentle, and a steep offset of one tenth of the drawn half-width, so a diverging run shows several growing zigzags before it leaves.
The slope arrow shows the gradient at 0.3 times its size and points uphill. The ball steps the opposite way. Changing a setting starts a new run, and the previous path stays as a faint ghost.
Real loss surfaces aren't perfect bowls, and their curvature changes during training. The 2 ÷ steepness threshold is exact only for this bowl. There is no noise or momentum.

findings.message: The 'Slope (uphill)' tag sits just above the readout line at the bottom edge of the frame. It is readable but cramped against the card text.
Near the minimum the slope arrow is a short stub (gradient × 0.3) and its 'Slope (uphill)' tag cannot be seen. That is honest scaling, but the learner loses the arrow's name here.
Not sampled: the zigzag-but-settle range (1/k to 2/k, which includes the default 0.3), the low end 0.01, and the effect of the steepness extremes. These captures do not verify them.

The plan and description promise that past the threshold 'each zigzag lands higher than the one before' and the ball then leaves. Here the run starts at steep offset 0.6 inside a drawn half-width of only 2/√k = 1. At rate 0.7 the first step lands at −1.08, so the run reads 'diverged' after 1 step and shows no growing zigzag at all. Even just above the threshold (0.55) it lasts only about 3 steps.

After diverging, the program sets the ball's height from the true loss (0.5·2.46+0.1 ≈ 1.33). The host clamps only x, to the rim, and the trail end is drawn at the rim height (≈1.10). So the ball floats visibly above and apart from the end of its own trail. Set the ball's height from the clamped point as well.

Same as the default view: at the high-end rate the run diverges in a single step, a straight line to the rim. No succession of growing zigzags is visible, so the promised overshoot pattern is never shown.
The ball hangs above the trail's end at the rim, because its height comes from the unclamped loss while the trail is drawn at the clamped rim height.
